Film Club just got bigger ⭐️🎬 Starting Thursday, April 9th, catch full-length episodes of PBS Film Club, now in its expanded home right here on PBS Documentaries. Join hosts Marissa Pina and Lucky Nguyen as they take the mic and dive deeper into their social commentary on documentaries you don’t want to miss.

The first episode drops tomorrow! Join the conversation all about "The Tallest Dwarf" :
and explore the complex world of the little people community, featuring guests Mark Povinell and Peet Montzingo. Let us know what films you hope Marissa and Lucky explore in the comments ⬇️

runs.text: You might notice things look a little different around here 👀 We’re excited to share that PBS Voices is now PBS Documentaries, a new home for powerful nonfiction storytelling from across our network, in partnership with

Starting TODAY, you’ll see feature-length films, short docs, science and history specials, and stories from communities across the country, all in one place. Check out our full trailer at the link above to see what’s coming!

Thanks for sticking with us as we begin this next chapter. We’re excited to bring a diverse collection of stories to the channel. We’re kicking things off with The Inquisitor, premiering today at 12 PM ET, which traces Barbara Jordan’s rise from Texas congresswoman to national icon, and highlights her powerful voice, integrity, and lasting impact on U.S. politics.

Now that we’ve got a new documentary home, what kinds of stories do you want to see next? Make sure to let us know in the comments! 👇

runs.text: “History is a verbal. You have to speak for people to know something.”

Yacouba Sissoko brings the ancient tradition of the griot to the next generation of African Americans. He refers to griots as “living history books,” who help keep the voices of ancestors alive through music. Catch up on The Story in Us and learn more about griot storytelling. Who taught you the stories, music, or traditions that shaped who you are? Share with us in the comments!

runs.text: This Women’s History Month, we’re taking a look at the women who reclaimed the stage of Peking Opera!

Peking Opera has been telling stories for centuries, with dazzling costumes, acrobatics, and fierce warrior women. But for much of the Qing Dynasty… women weren’t allowed on stage, and their roles were performed by men.

Today, that history has transformed, and the women who reclaimed the stage changed the art form forever. In The Story in Us, explore the untold story of warrior women in Chinese opera. Let us know what you think in the comments!

On this episode of The Story in Us, see how their homeland in the Sierra Tarahumara is kept alive through embroidery, as families create maps that represent home, history, and identity in the face of violence and displacement. In what ways do you preserve and keep memories? Share with us in the comments!

Southern stories are living on and being reimagined. runs.text: "My designs and patterns are inspired by my ancestors.” — Tasheena Littleben

For two Navajo weavers, each thread carries history, memory, and meaning. In the first episode of The Story in Us, weaving is more than an art form. It’s a practice of healing, strength, and connection to culture across generations. Through traditional techniques, their work tells a story that continues to evolve. Watch the first episode of The Story in Us and let us know what you think in the comments!
